'''''Cosmos caudatus''''' or '''king's salad'''<!--notable name used in certain English sources like the Australian Broadcasting Corporation: https://www.abc.net.au/gardening/factsheets/eat-your-greens/10972252--> is an [[annual plant]] in the genus ''[[Cosmos (plant)|Cosmos]]'', bearing purple, pink, or white [[ray florets]]. It is native to [[Latin America]] (from [[Rio Grande do Sul]] in southern Brazil to [[Tamaulipas]] in northeastern Mexico),<ref name=jenny>{{cite journal | vauthors = Melchert TE | title = Cosmos caudatus (Asteraceae: Coreopsideae) in Mexico: a cytotaxonomic reappraisal. | journal = Phytologia | location = USA | date = 1990 | volume = 69 | issue = 3 | pages = 200–215 | doi = 10.5962/bhl.part.17999 | url = https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/12982133#page/74/mode/1up | doi-access = free }} description, discussion, photographs, line drawings, distribution map</ref> and the [[West Indies]], though naturalized in tropical parts of Asia, Africa, and Australia.<ref>{{cite journal | veditors = Funk VA, Berry P, Alexander S, Hollowell TH, Kelloff CL | title = Checklist of the plants of the Guiana Shield (Venezuela: Amazonas, Bolivar, Delta Amacuro; Guyana, Surinam, French Guiana) | journal = United States National Herbarium | volume = 55 | pages = 1–584 | location = Washington, DC | publisher = National Museum of Natural History | date = July 2007 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | veditors = Jørgensen PM, León-YánezS | date = 1999 | title = Cat. Vasc. Pl. Ecuador. | journal = Monographs in Systematic Botany from the Missouri Botanical Garden | volume = 75 | pages = i–viii, 1–1181 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Humbert H | date = 1923 | title = Les Composées de Madagascar. | journal = Mémoires de la Société Linnéenne de Normandie | volume = 25 | pages = 1–335 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Sousa Sánchez M, Cabrera Cano EF | date = 1983 | title = Flora de Quintana Roo | journal = Listados Florísticos de México | volume = 2 | pages = 1–100 }}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis | vauthors = López Vargas A | date = 1995 | title = Estudio de Vegetación de las Partes Sud y Sudoeste de las Provincias Mizque y Campero --- Cochabamba | pages = i–vi, 1–152 | publisher = Universidad Mayor de San Simón, Cochabamba | degree = Ph.D }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Foster RC | date = 1958 | title = A catalogue of the ferns and flowering plants of Bolivia. | journal = Gray Herbarium of Harvard University | volume = 184 | pages = 1–223 }}</ref>

==Description==
The plant is known by several vernacular names in Central America which include:<ref name="FloraMesoamericana">{{Cite book|url=https://tropicos.org/name/2704081|title=Flora Mesoamericana|last1=Pruski|first1=John Francis|last2=Robinson|first2=Harold Ernest|publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden|year=2018|volume=5|location=St. Louis, Missouri|pages=i–xix, 1–608|chapter=Asteraceae|issue=2}}</ref>

{{div col}}
* ''chactsul'' ([[Yucatán]], [[Quintana Roo]])
* ''estrella del mar'' (Yucatán, Quintana Roo)
* ''cambray'' ([[Honduras]], El Salvador)
* ''cambray rojo'' (Honduras, El Salvador)
* ''mozote-doradilla'' (El Salvador)
* ''flor de muerto'' (Costa Rica)
{{div col end}}

The species grows up to {{convert|2|m|abbr=on}} in height.  The [[leaf|leaves]] are soft and pungent while the stem is light green with a purplish hue and succulent.  As night falls the leaves fold to close the terminal buds as the plant literally sleeps.  The flowers can be found solitary or in a loose clusters and are produced on a single stalk on auxiliary heads.<ref>{{cite book | vauthors = Hassan WE | date = 2006 | title = Healing Herbs of Malaysia | location = Kuala Lumpur | publisher = Federal Land Development Agency | isbn = 978-983-99544-2-5 }}</ref>

==Gastronomy==
''Cosmos caudatus'' is edible and its common names include '''''kenikir''''' (Indonesia) or '''''ulam raja''''' (in Malaysia, [[calque]]d as "the King's salad").<ref name = "BG"/> In [[Indonesian cuisine]] and [[Malaysian cuisine]], the leaves of this plant are used for ''[[ulam (salad)|ulam]]'', a type of traditional raw salad.  In Brunei, it was usually served with [[sambal]] (chilli paste) together with the local cuisine, [[ambuyat]]. It was brought by the Spaniards from [[Latin America]], via the Philippines, to the rest of [[Southeast Asia]].<ref name = "BG">{{cite book | vauthors = Bodeker G | date = 2009 | title = Health and Beauty from the Rainforest: Malaysian Traditions of Ramuan | location = Kuala Lumpur | publisher = Didier Millet | isbn = 978-981-4217-91-0 }}</ref>
